Introduction
The market has its own unique dynamics, and every movement is a burst of events — an instantaneous imprint of a shift in supply and demand. And the deeper we delved into the concept of event representations, the clearer it became that the
BAT
architecture seemed to have been designed specifically for this type of data. Its roots lie in the world of
event-based vision
, but its underlying logic is surprisingly well suited to the market. There are no frames here. There are only asynchronous streams — irregular, unpredictable, and infinitely varied. These streams must not merely be captured, but understood, structured, and turned into guides for decision-making.
We began by trying to identify the same structure in market movements that the authors of
BAT
find in the data stream from event cameras. And the
voxel-grid
concept they use aligns surprisingly well with our approach to handling financial data. In the original work, disorganized event noise is transformed into a dense, neatly organized cube of data. In it, time and space are woven into a single matrix. The same thing happens here, too. Ticks, volume spikes, and order book responses — we organize them into small temporal layers, transforming a chaotic stream into a structured grid that allows the model to operate on a solid foundation.
As a next step,
BAT
offers a multiscale view of movement. The market operates on several levels at once: in tiny price movements, in broad trend fluctuations, and in transitions between phases of volatility. And, like a seasoned analyst, the
BAT
architecture broadens its perspective by examining data from multiple angles simultaneously. It is delicate work. Small impulses often serve as the catalysts for large movements, while large shifts can mask microsegments of activity. Breaking the data down into multiple scales allows the framework to capture these transitions and form a more comprehensive view of the market.
However, the true power of
BAT
becomes apparent when the model begins to correlate events over time. The authors suggest using bidirectional temporal correlation — a concept very familiar to anyone who has ever tried to
get a feel for the market
in real time. To understand the current momentum, it is not enough to look only ahead. We need to see how the past connects with the future. Which structures remain stable, and which ones break down?
BAT
constructs a correlation tensor — a dense space that shows how well different time segments align with one another. The result is something like a map of market forces, where general trends, confirmations, divergences, and local distortions are evident.
But movement is never uniform. The pace of the market fluctuates — from a calm, slow flow to bursts of activity where milliseconds determine the outcome of a trade. It is precisely for these regimes that
BAT
uses adaptive temporal sampling, which can automatically adjust the analysis step size to match the nature of the current movement. When the market picks up speed, the model
compresses time
so as not to miss important transitions. Conversely, when the market quiets down, the model
widens the time window
, smoothing out the noise. As a result, the data stream is analyzed as if the system truly senses the market's rhythm, adapting to every new surge or lull.
Next, spatially adaptive aggregation comes into play. This is a form of feature cleaning and organization, where attention is focused not on all the data at once, but on those parts that actually drive the movement.
BAT
filters out outliers, discards inconsistent signals, and combines consistent elements into a single, stable representation of the dynamics. What we perceive in the market as
a clear price bias
or
a strengthening trend
materializes here as a
Motion-Feature
— a dense structure that reflects the true direction of movement.
Finally, the architecture uses iterative refinement to improve the motion estimate step by step. Just like an artist who first sketches the outline, then renders the form, light, and shadow. Each iteration makes the movement smoother, more precise, and more consistent, until the result is a reliable, fully developed solution. For the market, this means one thing: the model is able to view price movement as a structured process in which every impulse has its place and significance.
It is precisely this kind of architecture — sequential, multi-layered, and attentive to detail — that formed the basis of our own solution using
MQL5
tools. We create events, form temporal layers, establish correlations, adjust the time step, and organize dynamics into coherent structures. This is not simply a matter of transferring an idea from one field to another, but rather an organic adaptation of a technology that was originally developed in the world of asynchronous data. The market is also an
event camera
— only it measures liquidity rather than light. And
BAT
turned out to be a surprisingly accurate tool that allows us to look deeper. See not just the price, but its movement, context, and structure.
The author's visualization of the
BAT
framework is shown below.
Top-level Object
In our previous work, we have already presented our own approach to implementing the key elements of the
BAT
framework and examined, one by one, the logic behind event-based data preparation, multiscale encoding, temporal correlation, and dynamic modeling. Each component was a separate step, like a single stroke in a larger picture. Now is the time to bring the entire system together into a single, integrated whole that can function as a cohesive mechanism. That is precisely why our implementation includes a top-level object designed to integrate data preparation, feature engineering, contextual modeling, and the final aggregation of dynamics into a single architectural framework.
The
CNeuronBAT
class, built as an extension of the event-based convolutional block, serves as this integration point. This is not just a control wrapper, but a fully-fledged framework in which all previous ideas find their place. It combines the stages of preparing the
voxel
representation, encoding market events, establishing temporal relationships, and subsequently reconstructing movement, forming a data processing flow from the first tick to the final impulse.

The main functional units are concentrated within this object. The
cPrepare
data preparation module is responsible for the initial structuring of events — a sort of market
camera obscura
that transforms raw ticks into a neatly layered event volume. Next comes
cEncoder
, which generates a multiscale representation that allows the model to see what lies between volatility transitions and local bursts of activity. Working in conjunction with it is
cContext
, which is responsible for constructing bidirectional temporal correlations and forming a contextual space in which the model identifies stable relationships between signals.
The
cConcatenated
node plays a special role, combining data from different processing levels; the entire data stream then flows into
cGRU
— a two-dimensional event-based
GRU
block that serves as the heart of dynamic modeling. It is precisely here that the smoothing, refinement, and accumulation of the temporal structure — which is so essential for identifying the true direction of market movement — take place.
As we moved on to assembling a fully functional
BAT
module, it became clear that all our previous work had merely been preparation for creating a unified mechanism in which each element occupies its own strictly designated place. At the same time, the entire structure works like clockwork. In financial markets, where even the slightest delay or distortion in signal processing can prove costly, such architectural coherence is not merely a nice-to-have but a necessity. Therefore, in our top-level
BAT
object, we carefully assemble the entire technology stack, integrating individual components into a cohesive neural network section designed to analyze temporal dependencies, contextual relationships, and nonlinear market structures.

Only after the model's basic geometry has been securely established does the formation of the inner layers begin.
The data preparation module serves as the starting point for processing the quotes being analyzed. It includes normalization, through which the data passes in the same way that a traditional trader runs a stream of market values through checks, filters, and additional calculations before making a decision.

But the main action takes place a little further on. We create the
CreateFlow
component — a mechanism that converts discrete market sequences into a stream of spikes. This is not merely a formal format conversion, but a shift to an event-based representation of the data. Here, even the slightest price change becomes a brief electrical
click
. This representation makes the model more sensitive to market microstates and allows it to capture even the slightest fluctuations more accurately — fluctuations that often determine the outcome of a short-term trade.

To prevent this spike stream from breaking down into isolated events, we build a stack of historical data that serves as the
voxel
tensor proposed by the framework's authors. In this structure, each time step becomes a layer, and each unitary sequence becomes a separate face. The result is a compact yet surprisingly informative representation of the market context that helps the network perceive the spatial structure of market states. In it, local spikes and global trends coexist side by side.
The system then proceeds step by step to build the
Encoder
and
Context
branches — two parallel branches that will later merge and complement each other, forming a comprehensive understanding of what is happening in the market. Both branches are initialized with a set of windows of different sizes: the base
embed

This approach is a classic technique of multiscale convolution, which allows the model to consider both local fluctuations and broader market wave structures simultaneously. In trading, this is comparable to analyzing minute, hourly, and daily charts simultaneously: each provides its own insights, and only the overall picture reveals the market’s full intent.

Once the
Encoder
is complete, a crucial element of the authors' architecture for
BAT
comes into play —
bidirectional correlation
. It calculates the relationship between the forward and reverse directions of the time sequence. This allows the model to capture not only the familiar causal direction
past → future
, but also reverse dependencies arising from recurring market patterns. This is particularly important when it comes to financial data: the market often forms mirror-image patterns, and the ability to interpret them in both directions is a significant advantage.
index++;

Next is
SATMA
— an adaptive attention mechanism specifically refined by the authors of
BAT
for temporal sequences. It dynamically weights the significance of data segments, allowing the model to focus more on those price zones where real signals—rather than noise — are concentrated. In trading, this is similar to an experienced trader's habit of focusing not on every candle wick, but on key levels and areas of volume accumulation.

is fully assembled, its output is combined with the output of the context branch.

forms a unified data volume containing structural features, correlation relationships, and
attention
masks. This is now a
fusion
of information, ready for the final stage of analysis — processing by the

The
GRU
becomes a kind of nerve center for the
BAT
system. It is responsible for dynamics, memory, and state transitions, and it forms the final temporal representation that will be used by both the model and potential trading algorithms. In market terms, the
GRU
acts as the equivalent of an analyst who keeps recent patterns in mind, adjusts their significance, and takes market behavior over time into account.
The final step is data transposition — a careful rearrangement of the tensor's axes that brings the feature map into a form suitable for further processing.

After that, the BAT object can be considered fully initialized. The architecture is ready to perform a forward pass, update weights, operate in training mode, and save its state.
This is how the coherent, carefully designed
BAT
architecture takes shape — rigorous, well thought out, and rich in internal analytical mechanisms. It carefully combines multi-scale perception,
bidirectional connections
, and attention, transforming the chaotic flow of market data into a system of features capable of detecting market dynamics with the precision required by modern algorithmic trading.
Every component of the
CNeuronBAT
object is part of the overall lifecycle. And the entire computational flow proceeds strictly sequentially, as if a trading signal were being checked at every stage of the chain. The core logic is embedded in the forward pass method, which sets the entire mechanism in motion and coordinates data preparation, multiscale encoding, context analysis, and the generation of the final forecast.
bool
CNeuronBAT::feedForward(CNeuronBaseOCL *NeuronOCL)
  {
   CNeuronBaseOCL* current =
NULL
;
   CNeuronBaseOCL* prev = NeuronOCL;
//---
for
(
int
i =
0
; i < cPrepare.Total(); i++)
     {
      current = cPrepare[i];
if
(!current ||
         !current.FeedForward(prev))
return
false
;
      prev = current;
     }
The forward pass begins with the preparation block, where the data stream being analyzed sequentially passes through all the
cPrepare
elements. Each layer receives the results from the previous one, processes them, and passes them on—just as a trader first cleans the data, then checks for spikes in volume, and only then proceeds to a more in-depth analysis.
After preparation, the stream is routed to the
Encoder
branch. Here, it passes through all the components of
cEncoder
— multiscale convolutions,
residual
blocks, corrective
SpikeConv
modules, correlation layers, and adaptive layers. It is precisely at this point that a structural characterization of the market state takes shape: the model captures the geometry of movement, repeated pattern resonances, and the underlying structure of candlestick sequences.
for
(
int
i =
0
; i < cEncoder.Total(); i++)
     {
      current = cEncoder[i];
if
(!current ||
         !current.FeedForward(prev))
return
false
;
      prev = current;
     }
The algorithm then takes a subtle yet important step: it returns to the final node of the preparatory block and launches a parallel
Context
branch. Here, the same data is interpreted through a dynamic lens — with an emphasis on temporal dependencies, hidden delays, and the buildup of movement in a particular direction. This branch does not duplicate
Encoder
but complements it, allowing the model to view the market not only spatially but also from a causal-temporal perspective.
prev = cPrepare[-
1
];
for
(
int
i =
0
; i < cContext.Total(); i++)
     {
      current = cContext[i];
if
(!current ||
         !current.FeedForward(prev))
return
false
;
      prev = current;
     }
When both branches have finished processing, the merging phase begins. The outputs of
Encoder
and
Context
are combined into a single feature space using the
Concat
operation.
uint
units = cGRU.GetUnits();
if
(!Concat(cEncoder[-
1
].getOutput(), cContext[-
1
].getOutput(), cConcatenated.getOutput(),
              cEncoder[-
1
].Neurons() / units, cContext[-
1
].Neurons() / units, units))
return
false
;
if
(!cGRU.FeedForward(cConcatenated.AsObject()))
return
false
;
They are then sent to
cGRU
— the central recurrent node responsible for the final temporal data compression. It is here that the model
determines
which elements of the history matter now and which can be treated as market noise.
GRU
generates the final temporal trajectory of the market, carefully processing the simultaneous flow of structural and dynamic signals.
The next step is transposition. The
cTranspose
block formats the data as needed to integrate the result into the overall event representation format.
if
(!cTranspose.FeedForward(cGRU.AsObject()))
return
false
;
The next operation,
SumVecMatrix
, deserves special attention.
if
(!SumVecMatrix(cPrepare[
0
].getOutput(), cTranspose.getOutput(), cTranspose.getOutput(),
                    cPrepare[
0
].Neurons(),
1
,
0
,
0
,
0
,
1
))
return
false

At first glance, this looks like a typical
residual
step, but its significance runs much deeper. Our model is trained not to predict absolute values, but to capture and forecast flow dynamics. Changes in the market state, its trajectory, slope, and pace of movement. This is much closer to the actual logic of trading, where it is not the price level itself that matters, but rather the direction and strength of the momentum leading up to it.
That is why we do not use the final output of
GRU
directly. Instead, we sum it with the normalized representation of the latest market state obtained during the preparation stage. This process allows a relative dynamic forecast to be converted into absolute values that are familiar to the trader.
This technique makes the model's output more stable and closer to reality. We maintain a connection to the market's underlying structure while operating in the space of changes. This typically produces more stable, smoother, and economically meaningful forecast dynamics.
Only after all these steps are completed is the controlled stream sent to the parent
SpikeConvBlock
, completing the forward pass.
return
CNeuronSpikeConvBlock::feedForward(cTranspose.AsObject());
  }
Thus,
feedForward
operates as a tightly integrated pipeline: preparation → multiscale structure → dynamic context → recurrent compression → final transformation. The model receives a rich, multilayered representation of the market that accounts for both the shape of its movement and its pace, memory, direction, and local activity. Everything that distinguishes a meaningful trading signal from random fluctuations.
When the model first processes the data, it operates blindly — like a trader encountering an unfamiliar market for the first time. The parameters are random, the signals are chaotic, and the forecast results are far from reality. That is precisely why each forward pass is followed by a comprehensive
error-correction process
. This is a backpropagation procedure in which the model refines its own decisions step by step and adjusts its internal weights so that, next time, it responds to the data stream meaningfully rather than intuitively.
bool
CNeuronBAT::calcInputGradients(CNeuronBaseOCL *NeuronOCL)
  {
if
(!NeuronOCL)
return
false
;
//---
if
(!CNeuronSpikeConvBlock::calcInputGradients(cTranspose.AsObject()))
return
false
;
The algorithm begins with the spiking convolution decoding block. This element reconstructs the gradients at the input and feeds information back to the model about which specific features of the spiking cascade were incorrect. Next, the GRU module comes into play. It carefully extracts the gradients of the hidden states, evaluates the contribution of each time step, and feeds the corrective information back.
if
(!cGRU.CalcHiddenGradients(cTranspose.AsObject()))
return
false
;
At this stage, we restore the model’s understanding of the temporal structure of the stream — the very hidden patterns that, in real markets, determine shifts in momentum, the balancing of liquidity, or trend reversals.
The resulting gradients are combined into a single vector that passes through the concatenation node. Here, two independent sources of information —
context
and the
encoder
output — are separated and processed along their respective branches. This makes it possible to reconstruct the exact distribution of the error and avoid losing important relationships between local and global features of the market sequence.
if
(!cConcatenated.CalcHiddenGradients(cGRU.AsObject()))
return
false
;
uint
units = cGRU.GetUnits();
if
(!cEncoder[-
1
] || !cContext[-
1
] ||
      !DeConcat(cEncoder[-
1
].getGradient(), cContext[-
1
].getGradient(), cConcatenated.getGradient(),
                cEncoder[-
1
].Neurons() / units, cContext[-
1
].Neurons() / units, units))
return
false
;
   Deactivation(cEncoder[-
1
])
   Deactivation(cContext[-
1
])
A step-by-step backward pass then begins through all layers of the
encoder
— from the last to the first. Each layer compares its outputs with the gradients from the next node, adjusts its own parameters, and passes the updated gradient on.
CNeuronBaseOCL* current =
NULL
;
for
(
int
i = cEncoder.Total() -
2
; i >=
0
; i--)
     {
      current = cEncoder[i];
if
(!current ||
         !current.CalcHiddenGradients(cEncoder[i +
1
]))
return
false
;
     }
The context branch does the same: it handles the long-term structure of the data and, as if reaching back into history, helps the model refine the contribution of previous states.
for
(
int
i = cContext.Total() -
2
; i >=
0
; i--)
     {
      current = cContext[i];
if
(!current ||
         !current.CalcHiddenGradients(cContext[i +
1
]))
return
false
;

BAT
module develops a reliable ability to read the flow of market data. It learns to distinguish noise from structure, momentum from a random spike, and a reaction from a true trend. And while the model operates almost randomly at first, after many such backward passes, it becomes a tool capable of identifying patterns where the human eye sees only price turbulence.
Essentially,
CNeuronBAT
is the integration point where the event-driven approach becomes a full-fledged tool for analyzing financial data. We bring together all the ideas from the original
BAT

voxel

Model Architecture
After creating the top-level object of the
BAT,
framework, it makes sense to move on to the next step — designing the architecture of the trainable models. At this stage, we are once again going far beyond simply forecasting price movements. Our goal is to build a full-fledged trading
Agent
capable of independently analyzing context, recognizing market regimes, and making informed trading decisions in real time.
We retain the time-tested
Actor-Critic
training approach. This architecture has proven to be a practical solution for tasks that require interaction with a dynamic external environment. The
Actor
generates trading actions with the goal of maximizing strategic advantage. Meanwhile, the
Critic
is responsible for evaluating the quality of actions and adjusting the models' behavior. This dual-structure approach combines flexibility in decision-making with analytical rigor in evaluating results — qualities that are essential in the face of market uncertainty.
We incorporate the key ideas proposed by the authors of the
BAT
framework into the module responsible for processing the environment state — our market context
Encoder
. This module must transform raw data into a structured, compact, and meaningful representation of the current situation. Its performance determines how confidently the trading agent will navigate the flow of market data, distinguish sustained movements from short-term noise, and respond promptly to changes in liquidity, trend strength, or the nature of volatility.
Essentially, the
Encoder
serves as the voice of the market within the model — the link that transforms a chaotic stream of tick-by-tick changes and micro-patterns into a sequence of features suitable for strategic analysis. Integrating
BAT
principles allows this module to recognize dynamics, identify hidden relationships, and provide
the Actor
with
a comprehensive picture of what is happening
so it can make an informed decision.
The architecture of the trainable models is defined in a dedicated method called
CreateDescriptions
, which creates four key components:
Environment state
encoder
;
the
STFS
key feature extraction module, adapted from
S3CE-Net
(
Spike-guided Spatiotemporal Semantic Coupling and Expansion Network
);
a pair of models:
Actor
and
Critic
.
Essentially, what we are describing here is a framework that is subsequently populated with parameters and transformed into a fully-fledged trading decision-making mechanism.

It is particularly noteworthy that we have dispensed with the usual batch normalization layer. This is because the
BAT
module contains its own data preprocessing block, which already performs the necessary operations and ensures consistent feature scaling. Thus, additional normalization became redundant and could only complicate the data flow.
All other models have been carried over unchanged from previous work. They are fully compatible with the new architecture and continue to perform their functions of generating trading actions and evaluating their quality. You can find detailed information about them and their settings in the attachment, which includes the source code and parameters.
Testing
The final stage of our work is devoted to training the trading policy and testing it on real historical data. The first step was offline training using historical price data for the
EURUSD
currency pair on the
H
1 timeframe for the period from
January
2024 to
June
2025. This period served as a sort of training ground where the model learned to recognize historical patterns, analyze price dynamics and trading volumes, identify relationships between key features, and use those relationships to make forecasts. One could say that it developed its own
trader's intuition
, combined with mathematical rigor in data processing.
The next step — fine-tuning the model online in the
MetaTrader
5 Strategy Tester — allowed the model to adapt to the real-time data stream. Here, it learned the characteristics of
a live market
: it remained stable amid market noise, adjusted its actions when liquidity declined, and reacted instantly to sharp price spikes. This approach ensured a seamless integration of historical experience with current market signals, making trading decisions as timely and well-founded as possible.
The final test was conducted using data from
July
through
October 2025
, which was entirely new and had not been used previously in the training process. All model parameters were loaded without modification, which allowed for an objective assessment of the algorithm's ability to generalize and adapt to unfamiliar conditions. The results demonstrate that a step-by-step approach to training and adaptation enables the model to effectively analyze the market, forecast changes in key market features, and provide traders with a reliable basis for real-time decision-making.

USD

per trade. The maximum

These figures reflect not just dry statistics, but the dynamics of how the model
perceives the market
. Each trade was based on a careful assessment of the current market state and a forecast of key features. Linear regression of
equity
shows a correlation of
0.95
, confirming steady capital growth. Although the standard error reflects the natural volatility and market noise that any trading system faces,
the profit factor
and
Sharpe ratio
indicate that the strategy is capable of generating risk-adjusted returns. However, the short testing period and the small number of trades call for careful attention and a cautious approach.
It is particularly interesting that the model achieves positive results not through the number of winning trades, but through the quality of each profitable trade. The average profit significantly exceeds the average loss, which makes every successful entry a foundation for capital growth. At the same time, the maximum drawdown remains moderate. A
Recovery Factor
of
2.35
demonstrates that, following declines, the system is able to recover quickly while maintaining control over risk.
Despite these impressive results, we are aware of the potential risks. A short testing period, a limited number of trades, and a low
Z-score
suggest that some of the returns may have been due to a fortunate combination of circumstances. To improve reliability, additional analysis, checks, simulations, and stress tests are required, taking into account actual costs — such as spreads, commissions, and slippage. Only after successfully passing these tests can the strategy be considered ready for live trading.
Conclusion
In this article, we completed the development and testing of an integrated model based on the
BAT
framework for analyzing market data and formulating a trading policy. The systematic implementation of all components — from data preparation and market state encoding to the construction of the
Actor-Critic
model — has resulted in a system capable of making informed trading decisions based on a comprehensive analysis of key market features.
Backtesting on historical data showed positive returns and manageable risks. The model successfully extracted meaningful signals from a chaotic stream of quotes, generating capital growth with moderate drawdowns. An analysis of the metrics confirmed that the strategy is capable of balancing risk and return, identifying profitable opportunities, and responding to changes in market conditions.
It is particularly valuable that the
BAT
architecture and our module integration minimize the need for manual configuration and simplify system scaling. The strategy remains transparent and amenable to analysis and refinement, and the step-by-step approach to training and testing creates a solid foundation for the model's further development.
Despite the impressive results, we emphasize the need for additional robustness tests before applying the strategy in live trading. Only systematic and careful implementation can turn successes in testing into long-term achievements in the market.
Thus, the BAT framework presented here demonstrates significant practical value for building autonomous trading systems: it combines in-depth analysis, adaptability to market conditions, and scalability, creating a reliable platform for effective trading and further research in the field of algorithmic strategies.

against: The article describes a neural network architecture (BAT) for market analysis but does not specify any concrete trading signal — i.e., no rule defining *when to enter/exit*, no threshold, no condition on output (e.g., 'buy if output > 0.7'), no mapping from model output to actionable trade decision. It only states the model 'generates a latent representation' and is used within an 'Actor-Critic' agent, but the Actor’s decision logic (e.g., action selection policy, discretization of outputs, position sizing, or entry/exit conditions) is never defined in the text.

The article references 'Actor-Critic training' and says the Actor 'generates trading actions', but provides zero details on how actions are encoded (e.g., discrete: buy/sell/hold? continuous: lot size, TP/SL?), nor any formula, pseudocode, or even qualitative description of the action mapping — only that it's 'integrated' and 'compatible'. This violates requirement (2): the rule cannot be written as a precise formula because the entry/exit logic is entirely omitted.

The architecture relies on tick-level data ('ticks, volume spikes, and order book responses'), 'voxel-grid' built from 'ticks', 'spike stream' from 'discrete market sequences', and mentions 'order book responses' — all of which are unavailable in standard spot Forex (no real order book, no true tick volumes, no exchange-level bid/ask depth). This satisfies fatal criterion (3).
non_fatal: No out-of-sample test details beyond 'July–October 2025' — but per instructions, absence of OOS test is non-fatal.
No mention of spread, slippage, or commissions in testing — but per instructions, this is non-fatal.
Performance reported on EURUSD H1 only — limited instrument/timeframe scope, but not a fatal flaw.
Training uses historical data (Jan 2024–Jun 2025) and fine-tunes online — but no details on walk-forward validation or robustness across regimes — non-fatal per instructions.

judge.reject_reason: Статья описывает архитектуру нейросетевой модели BAT и её интеграцию в систему Actor-Critic, но не содержит чёткого, детерминированного правила входа: нет ни условия на выход модели (например, 'открыть лонг, если выход модели > порог'), ни описания, как выход модели преобразуется в торговое решение (дискретное действие, пороги, логика принятия решений). Также указано, что модель использует тиковые данные, волюмен-спайки и отклики стакана — данные, недоступные на стандартных спот-форекс барах (нет реального стакана, нет достоверных объёмов по тикам), что делает правило неприменимым на закрытых барах спот-форекса. Это фатальный порок.
judge.formula_and_logic: не указано — статья не описывает торговое правило, только архитектуру нейросети и общий контекст её использования в агенте Actor-Critic без деталей маппинга выхода в сигналы.
judge.author_oos_metrics: За 4 месяца (июль–октябрь 2025) депозит вырос с 100 до 209.25 USD (+109%), profit factor = 1.59, коэффициент восстановления = 2.35, максимальный просадок по equity = 20.2%, 90 сделок, 50% прибыльных, средняя прибыль/убыток = 6.56 / 4.13 USD.
judge.summary: Статья представляет нейросетевую архитектуру BAT, адаптированную для анализа рыночных событий через воксельные представления, многоуровневую обработку и двунаправленную корреляцию во времени. Модель интегрирована в Actor-Critic агента для автономной торговли, но конкретное торговое правило — условия входа, выхода или стопа — в тексте отсутствуют.
